section_1.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Conic Anatomy
section_1.content: Define a right circular cone and explain a 'planar section'—the shape created when a plane slices through the cone. Introduce the visual intuition of changing the angle of the cut to produce different shapes.
section_1.example: Imagine a flashlight beam hitting a wall: rotate the flashlight to see the spot transition from a perfect circle to an ellipse, a parabola, and finally a hyperbola.

section_2.title: Introducing Dandelin Spheres
section_2.content: Explain the concept of Dandelin spheres: small spheres placed inside the cone that are tangent to both the cone (along a circle) and the slicing plane (at a single point). These points are the 'Foci' of the conic section.
section_2.example: Think of a soap bubble trapped inside a funnel, perfectly touching the sides and being pinched by a flat glass sheet passing through the funnel.

section_3.title: The Geometric Proof: The Ellipse Case
section_3.content: Demonstrate why a planar slice is an ellipse using the Dandelin sphere. Show that the sum of distances from any point on the cut to the two focal points (the tangency points) is constant, proving the definition of an ellipse.
section_3.example: Use two 'contact points' on the plane where the spheres touch; draw a path of a ladybug crawling on the plane such that the total distance to these two points remains invariant, tracing an oval.

section_4.title: Visualizing Parabolas and Hyperbolas
section_4.content: Extend the logic: as the cutting plane becomes parallel to the side of the cone, one sphere is 'pushed' to infinity, resulting in a parabola. When the plane cuts through both nappes, two spheres are used to define the branches of a hyperbola.
section_4.example: Visualize a satellite dish (parabolic) receiving signals, where the 'receiver arm' points exactly toward the focal point defined by the hidden Dandelin sphere.

section_5.title: Synthesis & Real-world Application
section_5.content: Summarize how Dandelin spheres bridge the gap between 3D volume and 2D geometry. Conclude by connecting this to planetary orbits (ellipses) and reflective optics (parabolas).
section_5.example: A comet entering the solar system: it follows a path dictated by the same geometric laws that allow a telescope's mirror to focus starlight into a single, sharp point.
